stances.claim: ASEAN's failure to forge a strong united SCS stand was not unexpected -- consensus rule means a single negative blocks any decision, and member-states have divergent economic and political ties with China.
Self-interest is every nation's paramount concern -- the Philippines itself advances its own self-interest in claiming Kalayaan and Scarborough.
stances.rhetorical_move: even-handed realism applied equally to PH

stances.claim: No single individual or president can claim sole credit for protecting our maritime rights -- all administrations from Marcos through Duterte contributed to safeguarding the national interest.
The least Filipinos can do is avoid bickering and acts that defeat, dilute, or waive our legal rights -- and unite in preserving our patrimony for future generations.

notable_anecdotes: Brunei's reluctance explained: a huge amount of its oil -- the backbone of its economy -- is imported by China; if China reduces imports, Brunei's economy is severely affected.
The Marcos-era delegation's achievement: convincing 'coastal' states to accept archipelagic principles and a 200-NM EEZ -- far exceeding Hugo Grotius's 3-mile traditional limit.
RA 9522's last-minute passage in 2009 saving PH maritime claims from prescription -- a fact often overlooked in partisan critiques of the GMA administration.
J. Carpio's e-book 'Philippine Sovereign Rights and Jurisdiction in the West Philippine Sea' -- launched May 4, 2017 -- highlighted as a must-read accessible for free online.

decision_framework_signals: Apply the ASEAN-consensus rule as a structural constraint -- single-veto means aspirational unity must be won one bilateral relationship at a time
Assess each ASEAN member's SCS calculus through its primary economic dependency (Brunei/oil, Cambodia/aid) not just its stated political position
Credit multi-administration contributions when attributing national achievements -- avoids partisan distortion
Preserve all diplomatic options (Code of Conduct, bilateral negotiation, arbitral award) simultaneously -- do not abandon any
Treat RA 9522's prescription-beating passage as a critical but underappreciated legal milestone
one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why ASEAN's failure to forge a strong united SCS position against China was not unexpected: ASEAN operates by consensus, so a single dissent blocks any decision; of the seven SCS-bordering members, only Vietnam actively backs the arbitral award, while Brunei -- whose economy depends on Chinese oil imports -- and others are reluctant; the three non-SCS members (Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar) prioritize their China aid and trade relationships. He traces the multi-administration arc of PH maritime rights: the Marcos-era delegation won archipelagic principles and a 200-NM EEZ in the UNCLOS negotiations; GMA's last-minute passage of RA 9522 in 2009 saved our claims from prescription (upheld in Magallona v. Ermita per J. Carpio); Aquino III's administration won the arbitral award; Ramos and Estrada contributed by grounding a vessel at Ayungin Shoal. Duterte's 'independent foreign policy,' direct negotiations with China, and proposed Asean-China Code of Conduct continue the chain. The author's thesis: no single president can claim sole credit -- all contributed. He closes with a civic-unity prescription: avoid bickering and acts that defeat, dilute, or waive our legal rights, and unite in preserving our patrimony for future generations. He plugs J. Carpio's free-access e-book on the WPS dispute, launched May 4.
